content.text: Land Rover Discovery 3 276DT 2.7 TDV6 Crankshaft Failure Representative Case Study Land Rover Discovery 3 TDV6 Crankshaft Failure — Why Ignoring a Rumble at 142,000 Miles Cost £7,600 A premium visual breakdown of how a subtle rumble under load became a snapped crankshaft, destroyed bottom end, and a £7,610 reconditioned engine replacement. “I heard a rumble under load when towing the caravan. It was subtle — I thought it might be a wheel bearing or exhaust heat shield. I ignored it for a few weeks. Then one morning on the M6, there was a loud bang from the engine bay, the oil pressure light flashed, and the accelerator pedal went dead. By the time I coasted to the hard shoulder, the engine had locked solid. The AA man said, ‘That’s not a bearing — that’s a snapped crank.’” Compare TDV6 Repair Quotes See the Failure Timeline 138k First rumble 142k Snapped crank 4,000 mi From rumble to failure £7,610 Final repair 12–24 mo Warranty Case summary A 2007 Land Rover Discovery 3 with 142,000 miles and a crankshaft that was already failing. At 138,000 miles the owner heard a subtle rumble under load when towing. He ignored it for a few weeks. At 142,000 miles, the crankshaft snapped at motorway speed, destroying the 2.7 TDV6 engine beyond repair. Model Land Rover Discovery 3 (2007) Engine 276DT 2.7 TDV6 V6 diesel First symptom 138,000 miles Failure mileage 142,000 miles Service history Independent specialist every 10,000 miles Primary use Family car, towing caravan, off-road use Disclaimer: This is an illustrative representative scenario based on workshop consensus and known 276DT failure patterns [INDUSTRY ESTIMATE]. Individual outcomes vary. Early warning The whole disaster started with a subtle rumble under load. The sound was most noticeable when towing uphill. The owner dismissed it as a wheel bearing or exhaust heat shield. Within 4,000 miles, the crankshaft snapped, destroying the engine. What owner thought “Probably a wheel bearing” The vehicle still drove normally, so the symptom did not feel urgent. What it actually was Bottom-end bearing wear The TDV6 crank bearings were wearing, allowing the crank to flex and eventually snap. Why it matters Catastrophic snap Once the crank snaps, the block is destroyed. Land Rover does not authorise third-party rebuilds. If your Discovery 3 TDV6 develops a rumble under load — especially when towing — have the bottom end inspected immediately. Ignoring it can lead to a snapped crankshaft and a £7,000+ engine replacement. Failure timeline From a subtle rumble to a snapped crank in just 4,000 miles. This case is a classic catastrophic TDV6 crankshaft failure: the owner ignored the warning signs and paid the price. What the owner noticed A subtle rumble under load became a snapped crankshaft at 65mph within 4,000 miles. What was happening internally Bottom-end bearings wore, the crank flexed and snapped, destroying the block and oil system. “I nearly scrapped it. The repair cost more than the car was worth on paper. But what was I going to buy for £7,600- Another Discovery 3 with unknown history and the same risk- A reconditioned engine at least came with a warranty. I bit the bullet and paid £7,600 to keep it on the road. Two years later, it’s still going strong.” 138,000 miles Subtle rumble under load 142,000 miles Snapped crank at 65mph Specialist Reconditioned engine fitted Workshop diagnosis The snapped crank and metal debris told the full story. The specialist drained the oil and found metal particles throughout. The crankshaft had snapped between two main bearing journals, destroying the block. Oil condition Thick, black, containing metallic particles Oil filter Full of metal debris Crankshaft Snapped — complete failure between two main bearing journals Connecting rods One bent, one snapped Cylinder block Damaged — beyond repair Oil pump Destroyed by debris Turbocharger Unknown condition — potential debris contamination Specialist summary “The crankshaft has snapped. This is a catastrophic bottom-end failure. Land Rover does not allow these engines to be rebuilt satisfactorily by third parties — the block is destroyed, and the crank is in two pieces. You need a full replacement engine.” Repair options Scrap, used engine, reconditioned exchange, or Land Rover new engine. Compare the routes the owner faced after diagnosis. The reconditioned long engine is selected by default because that was the chosen route. Scrap Used Engine Reconditioned Land Rover New Total loss Scrap the Discovery £500–£1,500 Sell as spares/repair. A Discovery 3 with a snapped crankshaft is a total loss for most private sellers. Scope Used 276DT TDV6 from breaker Supply cost £2,000–£3,500 Fitted cost (indie) £3,500–£5,500 Warranty 30–90 days typical Lead time 5–10 days Best for Budget-limited owners accepting higher risk Chosen route Reconditioned Long Engine (Exchange) £7,500–£10,000 Fully reconditioned 276DT long engine — with snapped crank surcharge if core not returnable. Scope Fully reconditioned 276DT long engine (cylinder head, block, crankshaft, pistons, bearings) Supply cost £6,500–£8,500 Fitted cost (indie) £7,500–£10,000 Surcharge for snapped crank Additional £1,000–£1,500 (core charge not refundable if crank is snapped) Warranty 12–24 months (specialist dependent) Lead time 7–14 days Best for Owners committed to keeping the Discovery long-term Dealer route Land Rover New Engine £11,000–£15,000+ New genuine Land Rover crate engine — dealer policy for catastrophic failure. Scope New genuine Land Rover crate engine Cost (supply only) £8,000–£12,000+ Fitted cost (dealer) £11,000–£15,000+ Warranty 24 months (Land Rover) Lead time 14–28 days Best for Insurance claims or owners who insist on genuine parts regardless of cost The uncertainty play The replacement engine was not the only question. Debris had circulated through the oil system. With metal particles throughout the oil system, the specialist could not fully know whether the turbocharger had already been affected by debris contamination. Path A Fit reconditioned long engine only. Keep existing turbocharger. £7,600 If turbo fails later: add £800–£1,200 + labour. Path B Fit reconditioned long engine + new turbocharger. £8,800 Higher upfront cost, but eliminates turbo failure risk. The owner chose Path A due to budget constraints — an extra £1,200 for a new turbo was difficult to justify immediately. Key takeaway: if budget allows, replace the turbo preventatively when fitting a replacement engine. Fork in the road The owner ignored the rumble. Then the crank snapped on the motorway. The vehicle was worth approximately £5,000–£8,000 before failure. A £7,600 reconditioned engine exceeded the vehicle's value on paper — but replacing the Discovery with a comparable 4x4 would cost £15,000–£25,000+. Scrap the Discovery Path 1 Sell as spares/repair. An exchange engine is the only game in town.” Lessons learned If your Discovery 3 TDV6 develops a rumble under load, do not ignore it.
